title: Does Alcohol Cause Kidney Stones? Beer, Uric Acid and Risk
excerpt: Does drinking cause kidney stones? What large studies found about beer and wine, how alcohol raises uric acid, which drinks and mixers to watch, and when kidney pain needs a doctor.
metaDescription: Does alcohol cause kidney stones? What studies found about beer and wine, how drinking raises uric acid, which mixers to avoid, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** alcohol is not a direct cause of kidney stones. In fact, several large long-term studies found that people who drank moderate amounts of beer or wine had a somewhat *lower* rate of stones than people who didn't. That doesn't make alcohol good for your kidneys. Heavy drinking can still push you toward stones in indirect ways: it can leave you dehydrated, it raises uric acid (a waste product that can crystallize into stones), and it tends to come with sugary mixers, salty bar food, and weight gain, all of which are real risk factors. Whether alcohol helps or hurts your stone risk depends on how much you drink, what you drink it with, and what kind of stones you're prone to.

**The quick rules:** If you've had a kidney stone before, the most useful single habit is drinking enough water to keep your urine pale, especially on nights you drink. Have a glass of water with each alcoholic drink. Go easy on beer if you've had uric acid stones or gout. Skip cola and sugary-soda mixers where you can. And if you're passing a stone right now, hold off on alcohol until your doctor says otherwise.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article explains general research and is not a substitute for medical advice. **Get urgent care (emergency room or call 911) if** you have severe pain in your side or back along with fever or chills, you can't keep fluids down because of vomiting, you can't pass urine, you have only one working kidney, or the pain is so bad that nothing helps. A stone that blocks the kidney while there's an infection behind it is a medical emergency. **Book a regular appointment if** you've had a stone before and want to prevent the next one, you see blood in your urine, you get repeated pain in your side after drinking, or you have gout. A doctor can test your urine and any stone you pass to work out exactly which type you make, and that changes the advice.

## How Kidney Stones Form (In Plain Words)

Your urine carries dissolved waste: calcium, oxalate, uric acid, phosphate, and others. As long as there's enough water to keep them dissolved, they pass out of you without trouble. When urine gets too concentrated, or when one of those substances shows up in large amounts, it can start to form tiny crystals. Those crystals can stick together and grow into a stone.

There are several types, and the type matters because each one has slightly different triggers:

| Stone type | How common | What tends to drive it |
|---|---|---|
| **Calcium oxalate** | By far the most common type | Low urine volume, a lot of salt, high-oxalate foods eaten without calcium, low citrate in the urine |
| **Calcium phosphate** | Less common | Low urine volume, certain metabolic and kidney conditions |
| **Uric acid** | A smaller but meaningful share | High uric acid, acidic urine, low urine volume, high purine intake (meat, seafood, beer), obesity, diabetes, gout |
| **Struvite** | Uncommon | Certain urinary tract infections |
| **Cystine** | Rare | An inherited condition |

Across all of these, one factor shows up again and again: **not making enough urine.** Concentrated urine is the common soil every stone grows in. That's why the alcohol question really comes down to two things: does drinking leave you with more fluid or less, and does it change the chemistry of your urine?

## So Does Alcohol Cause Kidney Stones?

Not directly. There's no single substance in alcohol that turns into a stone. The relationship is indirect, and it works in both directions.

### What the big studies found

The best long-term data come from large American cohort studies that tracked the health and habits of tens of thousands of nurses and male health professionals for years, including the Nurses' Health Studies and the Health Professionals Follow-up Study. Researchers at Harvard, led by Gary Curhan's group, used these cohorts to look at how different drinks related to kidney stones. A widely cited 2013 analysis in the *Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology* found that people who drank beer and wine had a lower risk of developing stones than people who didn't, while people who drank sugar-sweetened sodas had a higher risk. Coffee, tea, and orange juice were also linked to lower risk.

A separate study in Finland, following a large group of middle-aged male smokers, also found that beer drinkers had fewer kidney stones.

These are observational studies. They show patterns, not cause and effect, and moderate drinkers can differ from non-drinkers in lots of ways. But the consistent finding is that moderate beer and wine drinking was **not** linked to more stones.

### Why moderate drinking might look protective

The most likely explanation is plain fluid. A pint of beer or a glass of wine is mostly water, and alcohol makes you urinate more. More urine means more dilute urine, and dilute urine is less likely to form crystals. Some researchers have also suggested that compounds in beer, such as hops, might slow calcium loss from bone or affect crystal formation, but that's speculative.

### Why heavy drinking is a different story

The studies above are about moderate intake. Heavy and binge drinking change the picture in a few ways:

- **Dehydration.** Alcohol blocks a hormone called vasopressin (also called antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. With it switched off, you pee out more than you'd expect. If you drink a lot of strong alcohol and little water, you can end the night with less fluid in your body than you started with. The next morning, when you wake up thirsty with dark urine, your urine is at its most concentrated. Our guide on [why alcohol makes you pee](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-pee) explains this hormone effect in more detail.
- **Higher uric acid.** Alcohol raises uric acid levels, which is the main concern for uric acid stones (more on this below).
- **Everything that comes with it.** Late-night salty food, sugary mixers, and the weight gain that often comes with regular heavy drinking all raise stone risk on their own.

So the fair summary is this: **moderate drinking with enough water hasn't been linked to more stones, but heavy drinking, little water, and the habits around it can push your risk up.**

## Alcohol and Uric Acid: The Real Link to Stones

If there's one type of stone where alcohol clearly matters, it's uric acid stones. This is also why alcohol is a known trigger for gout, which is caused by the same substance crystallizing in the joints.

Uric acid is a waste product your body makes when it breaks down purines. Purines come from two places: your own cells, and food and drink. Alcohol raises uric acid in three ways:

1. **It speeds up production.** When your liver processes alcohol, it burns through energy molecules in a way that leaves behind more purine breakdown products, which become uric acid.
2. **It slows removal.** Processing alcohol raises lactic acid in your blood. Your kidneys handle lactic acid and uric acid through overlapping routes, so when there's a lot of lactic acid around, less uric acid gets cleared into the urine.
3. **Beer adds its own purines.** Beer is unusually rich in purines because of the yeast and grain it's made from. That's why beer has the strongest link to gout of any drink, and why it's the drink most worth limiting if you form uric acid stones. Wine appears to have a weaker effect on uric acid than beer or spirits in gout research.

Uric acid crystallizes most easily when urine is both **concentrated** and **acidic**. People with obesity, type 2 diabetes, or metabolic syndrome tend to have more acidic urine, which is part of why those conditions raise the risk of uric acid stones. If you drink heavily and also have one of these conditions, the effects stack up.

The encouraging part: uric acid stones are the one common type that can often be dissolved with treatment. Doctors sometimes prescribe a medicine such as potassium citrate to make urine less acidic, and some people need a drug that lowers uric acid production. That's a conversation for your doctor, and it's another reason to find out what kind of stone you actually have.

If you have gout as well as stones, your doctor may give you more specific advice about alcohol, because the two conditions share the same root.

## Is Beer Good for Kidney Stones?

This is one of the most common questions, and there's a popular belief that beer helps "flush" stones out. Here's what's true and what isn't.

**What's true:**

- Beer is mostly water and makes you urinate more, which dilutes the urine.
- In large observational studies, moderate beer drinkers had fewer stones than non-drinkers.

**What isn't supported:**

- There is no good evidence that drinking beer helps you pass a stone you already have. The idea comes from the fact that beer makes you pee, but water does that without the alcohol.
- Beer isn't a treatment or a prevention plan. Doctors don't recommend starting to drink to lower stone risk.
- For people who form uric acid stones or have gout, beer is the drink most likely to make things worse because of its purine content.

**The practical takeaway:** if you already enjoy a beer now and then and you've had calcium oxalate stones, moderate beer drinking isn't something the research flags as a problem, as long as you're drinking enough water overall. If you've had uric acid stones or gout, beer is the first thing to cut back. Either way, water does the useful part of what beer does, with none of the downsides.

## Which Drinks Are Better or Worse for Kidney Stones?

Here's a rough guide based on what the research and stone-prevention guidance suggest. It's general, and your own stone type may change it.

| Drink | What to know |
|---|---|
| **Water** | The foundation of stone prevention. Nothing else beats it. |
| **Wine** | Linked to lower stone risk in large studies. Weaker effect on uric acid than beer. Still dehydrating in large amounts. |
| **Beer** | Linked to lower overall stone risk in large studies, but high in purines. Limit it if you form uric acid stones or have gout. |
| **Spirits (neat or on the rocks)** | Adds alcohol with very little fluid. If you drink spirits, pair them with water. |
| **Spirits with sugary soda** | The weakest combination. Sugar-sweetened sodas have been linked to higher stone risk on their own. |
| **Spirits with soda water and lime or lemon** | A better mixer choice. Citrus juice adds citrate, which helps stop crystals forming. |
| **Hard seltzers** | Mostly water and fairly low in sugar. No specific stone research, but similar logic to a spirit with soda water. |
| **Cocktails with fruit juice or syrups** | Depends on the sugar content. Very sweet cocktails carry the same concern as sugary soda. |

### The mixer problem

People rarely think about this, but the mixer can matter as much as the alcohol. In the Harvard beverage research, sugar-sweetened sodas were linked to a higher risk of stones. Fructose, the sugar in table sugar and high-fructose corn syrup, raises uric acid and may increase calcium and oxalate in the urine. Colas also contain phosphoric acid. A rum and Coke, a whiskey and cola, or a run of sweet cocktails therefore combines alcohol with a known stone risk factor.

If you want a lower-risk mixer, soda water with fresh lemon or lime is a good choice. Citrate from citrus fruit binds to calcium in the urine and helps stop crystals growing, which is why lemon water is sometimes suggested for people with calcium stones. For more on picking a mixer, see our look at [soda for a hangover](/never-hungover/soda-for-hangover).

## Kidney Pain After Drinking: Stone or Something Else?

A lot of people search for kidney stones after waking up with a sore back or side after a night out. Most of the time it isn't a stone. But it's worth knowing the difference.

**Pain that usually isn't a stone:**

- A dull ache across the lower back, often from sleeping in an odd position, dehydration, or general hangover aches.
- Mild soreness that eases with water, rest, and food over a few hours.
- Muscle aches after dancing, standing for hours, or a fall.

**Pain that suggests a stone:**

- Sudden, sharp, severe pain in your side or back just below the ribs, often on one side.
- Pain that moves toward your lower belly or groin as the stone travels.
- Pain that comes in waves and doesn't ease when you change position. Many people describe it as one of the worst pains they've ever had.
- Pink, red, or brown urine, or a burning feeling when you pee.
- Needing to pee often but only passing small amounts.
- Nausea or vomiting along with the pain.

**Other kidney-related causes worth knowing about:**

- **Kidney infection.** Pain in the side with fever, chills, and feeling very unwell needs prompt care.
- **Alcohol-related muscle breakdown.** Very rarely, a heavy binge, especially with intense exercise, heat, or lying still for hours, can cause muscle damage that releases a protein into the blood that strains the kidneys. Signs include severe muscle pain and very dark, cola-colored urine. That needs a doctor quickly.

If you get pain in your side regularly after drinking, even if it's mild, it's worth mentioning to a doctor. Our broader guide to [alcohol and kidney health](/never-hungover/alcohol-kidney-disease-renal-function-impact-2025) covers how heavy drinking affects the kidneys over time.

## Can You Drink Alcohol While Passing a Kidney Stone?

It's best not to. There are a few clear reasons:

- **Dehydration works against you.** Your goal while passing a stone is steady urine flow. Drinking alcohol makes you pee more in the moment, but it can leave you with less fluid overall, especially if you're also vomiting.
- **It can make nausea worse.** Stone pain often comes with nausea. Alcohol irritates the stomach and adds to it.
- **It doesn't mix well with the usual stone medicines.**
  - **Opioid painkillers** sometimes prescribed for stone pain should not be combined with alcohol. Together they can dangerously slow breathing.
  - **NSAIDs** such as ibuprofen, naproxen, or ketorolac are commonly used for stone pain. Alcohol raises their risk of stomach irritation and bleeding, and both can stress the kidneys when you're short on fluid.
  - **Tamsulosin** (Flomax) is often prescribed to help a stone pass. It can cause dizziness and lightheadedness, especially when standing up, and alcohol can add to that.
- **It can hide warning signs.** Being drunk or hungover can make it harder to notice fever, worsening pain, or not peeing, which are the signs that need urgent attention.

Stick to water while you're passing a stone, follow your doctor's instructions on pain relief, and ask them when it's fine to drink again. If you're unsure whether a painkiller is safe with alcohol, our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) covers acetaminophen, and a pharmacist can check any other medicine for you.

## Can Alcohol Cause Kidney Stones in People Who Have Never Had One?

It can play a part, but rarely on its own. The people most at risk from the combination are those who already have other risk factors:

- A **family history** of kidney stones.
- **Gout** or high uric acid.
- **Obesity, type 2 diabetes, or metabolic syndrome.**
- A diet high in **salt, red meat, or sugary drinks**.
- **Low daily fluid intake**, or a lot of sweating from heat, exercise, or a physical job.
- Certain **bowel conditions** or past weight-loss surgery, which can raise oxalate absorption.

If you drink heavily and tick a few of these boxes, alcohol is one more push in the wrong direction. If you drink moderately, drink plenty of water, and don't have these risk factors, alcohol is unlikely to be what decides whether you get a stone.

## How to Drink Without Raising Your Stone Risk

Whether you've had a stone before or just want to keep it that way, these habits have the best support. None of them require giving up alcohol entirely if you drink moderately, though cutting back always helps.

### 1. Drink water alongside alcohol

Have a full glass of water with each alcoholic drink and another before bed. This offsets the extra urine alcohol makes you produce. The American Urological Association's guideline for people who have had stones recommends enough fluid to make at least 2.5 liters of urine a day, which for most people means drinking more than that. Pale yellow urine is a reasonable everyday sign you're getting enough. Our guide on [whether water helps a hangover](/never-hungover/does-water-help-a-hangover) covers what water can and can't do the morning after.

### 2. Rehydrate the morning after

Your urine is often most concentrated the morning after drinking. Start the day with water before coffee. If you've sweated a lot or been sick, an oral rehydration drink can help replace fluid and salts, though for stone formers it's worth choosing a low-sugar option. See our guide to [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) for what's worth it and what's marketing.

### 3. Choose your mixer carefully

Swap cola and sugary sodas for soda water with lemon or lime. Watch out for very sweet cocktails.

### 4. Go easy on beer if you form uric acid stones

If you've had uric acid stones or gout, beer is the drink to cut first. Pair this with moderating red meat, organ meats, and some seafood, which are also high in purines.

### 5. Watch the late-night food

Salty foods like fries, chips, pizza, and cured meat increase how much calcium your kidneys put into urine. One salty snack won't matter much, but a regular pattern does.

### 6. Don't cut calcium from food

This surprises people. For calcium oxalate stone formers, eating normal amounts of calcium from food usually *lowers* risk, because calcium binds oxalate in the gut before it's absorbed. Cutting dairy to avoid stones generally backfires. Calcium supplements are a different matter, so ask your doctor about those.

### 7. Keep an eye on the overall pattern

The current US Dietary Guidelines define moderate drinking as up to one drink a day for women and up to two for men. Staying near that range, rather than saving drinks up for a big weekend binge, avoids the worst of the dehydration and uric acid spikes.

## Does Anything Else Help? A Note on Supplements

Some people with a history of stones take supplements or remedies. The evidence varies a lot:

- **Potassium citrate** is a prescription treatment with good evidence for certain stone types. It's not something to start on your own.
- **Lemon juice and lemon water** add some citrate. It's a cheap, reasonable habit, though less potent than prescription citrate.
- **Vitamin C in high doses** can be converted to oxalate, and high-dose vitamin C supplements have been linked to more stones in men in observational research. If you form calcium oxalate stones, ask your doctor before taking large doses.
- **Cranberry products** are often suggested for urinary health but there is no good evidence they prevent kidney stones.

### Where DHM fits

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. It's what this site focuses on, so it's worth being clear: **there is no good evidence that DHM prevents kidney stones or protects the kidneys from them.** Most of the DHM research is from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. It does not change your need to drink water, and it's no reason to drink more.

What some people use it for is feeling better the morning after a night out. If that's your interest, take it as an add-on to the habits above, not a replacement for them. Popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you have kidney disease or take regular medication, check with your doctor before adding any supplement.

For the habits with the best evidence for an easier morning, our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) is the place to start.

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol isn't a direct cause of kidney stones. Large studies linked moderate beer and wine drinking to slightly *fewer* stones, most likely because of the extra fluid.
- Heavy drinking can still raise your risk through dehydration, higher uric acid, sugary mixers, salty food, and weight gain.
- Beer is the drink most worth limiting if you form uric acid stones or have gout, because it's high in purines.
- Sugar-sweetened sodas, including cola mixers, have been linked to more stones. Soda water with lemon or lime is a better mixer.
- The most useful habit by far is water: a glass with each drink, one before bed, and enough through the day to keep your urine pale.
- If you're passing a stone, skip alcohol and follow your doctor's advice on pain relief. Pain with fever or chills, or not being able to pee, needs urgent care.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does alcohol cause kidney stones?**

Alcohol is not a direct cause of kidney stones, and in large long-term studies moderate beer and wine drinkers actually had a somewhat lower rate of stones than non-drinkers. Heavy drinking can still raise your risk indirectly by leaving you dehydrated, raising uric acid levels, and coming packaged with sugary mixers, salty snacks, and weight gain. The biggest single factor for most people is not making enough urine, so water intake matters far more than the drink itself.

**Is beer good for kidney stones?**

Beer is not a treatment for kidney stones. Some large observational studies linked moderate beer drinking to fewer stones, probably because it adds fluid and makes you urinate more. But beer is also high in purines, which raise uric acid, so it can work against people prone to uric acid stones or gout. There is no good evidence that drinking beer helps pass a stone, and plain water does the useful part without the downsides.

**Can I drink alcohol if I have a kidney stone right now?**

It's best to avoid it while you're passing a stone or waiting for treatment. Alcohol can leave you more dehydrated, it can worsen nausea, and it doesn't mix well with common stone medicines such as opioid painkillers, NSAIDs like ibuprofen or ketorolac, and tamsulosin, which can cause dizziness on its own. Drink water instead and ask your doctor when it's safe to have alcohol again.

**Which alcoholic drinks are worst for kidney stones?**

The drinks most worth limiting are the ones that combine alcohol with other known risk factors: beer if you tend to form uric acid stones or have gout, and cocktails or highballs made with sugary soda, especially cola. In studies of beverages and stone risk, sugar-sweetened sodas were linked to a higher risk while wine and beer were not. Drinking spirits neat without any water alongside is also unhelpful because it adds little fluid.

**How do I know if pain after drinking is a kidney stone or just a hangover?**

Hangover aches are usually dull, spread out, and improve with rest, food, and fluids. Kidney stone pain is typically sharp and severe, sits in your side or back just below the ribs, often moves toward the lower belly or groin, and comes in waves. Blood in the urine, pain when peeing, or nausea with that kind of pain points toward a stone. Pain with fever or chills needs urgent medical care.

**Does alcohol raise uric acid?**

Yes. Alcohol speeds up the breakdown of compounds in the body that produce uric acid, and it also makes the kidneys clear uric acid less efficiently. Beer adds an extra load because it contains purines from yeast and grain. Higher uric acid in the urine, especially when the urine is concentrated and acidic, is the setup for uric acid stones.

**How much water should I drink to avoid kidney stones if I drink alcohol?**

Urology guidelines for people who have had stones aim for enough fluid to produce about 2.5 liters of urine a day, which for most people means drinking more than that. On drinking days, a simple habit is a glass of water with each alcoholic drink and another before bed. Pale yellow urine is a reasonable sign you're on track. If you have heart or kidney problems, ask your doctor what amount is right for you.

**Does DHM help prevent kidney stones?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents kidney stones in people. DHM is studied mainly for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver, and most of that research is in animals. If you form stones, the measures with real evidence are drinking more water, cutting back on salt and sugary drinks, moderating meat and beer if you form uric acid stones, and following your doctor's advice.
